The result is a table with the columns id, label, type, and degree: one row per node sorted by id, type empty (null), and degrees 2, 3, 3, 2." width="100%"} Exports all nodes and their attributes to a Polars DataFrame for tabular analysis. Each row represents a node, with columns for the node ID and any attributes set on nodes. The DataFrame always includes 'id', 'label', and 'type' as the first three columns, sorted by `id` in ascending order. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [pl.DataFrame]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A Polars DataFrame with mandatory columns 'id', 'label', 'type' (first three), followed by other attributes and 'degree'. If the graph has no nodes, the frame has no rows but still has the 'id', 'label', 'type' and 'degree' columns. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The column layout is deliberately stable so downstream code never has to guess: `id`, `label`, and `type` always come first (in that order), any custom node attributes follow in alphabetical order, and a computed `degree` column always closes the frame. Rows come sorted by `id` ascending. Missing values, whether an absent label, a node without the `type` attribute, or an attribute present on some nodes but not others, are represented as `None`, so Polars operations that respect nulls behave as expected. A Polars column has one data type, so an attribute whose values differ in type from node to node is reconciled: integers beside floats become floats, and single values beside lists become one-item lists (a node read from Cypher's `(:Person:Actor)` has the `type` `["Person", "Actor"]`, so a plain `"Person"` beside it reads `["Person"]`). Any other mix, such as a string beside a number, gives an `Object` column that holds the values unchanged. The `id`, `label` and `degree` columns always hold the node IDs, labels and degrees: an attribute with one of those names (such as the `degree` that `degrees()` stores, or a Graphviz `label` read by `from_dot()`) is left out of the table. Read it with `get_node_attrs()` instead. ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~get_edge_df`) : The edges as a Polars DataFrame. [](`~get_node_attrs`) : One attribute as a dictionary, including any the frame leaves out. [](`~set_node_attrs`) : Write values computed in Polars back onto the nodes. ## Examples {.doc-examples} The frame has a row per node, sorted by ID. `id`, `label` and `type` come first, then the stored attributes in alphabetical order, then each node's degree: ::: {#9c42c8bd .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph.from_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C")]) graph.set_node_attrs("score", {"A": 95, "B": 88}) graph.get_node_df() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}
shape: (3, 5)

1"A"null951

``` ::: ::: "C" has no `score`, so its value is null. ### Hubs and bridges Zachary's karate club split in two after a dispute between its instructor (member 0) and its administrator (member 33). Storing two centralities on the graph puts them in the node frame side by side, ready for Polars: ::: {#9874c9e7 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import polars as pl karate = ec.karate_club() karate.betweenness_centrality(attr_name="betweenness") karate.pagerank(attr_name="pagerank") nodes = karate.get_node_df() nodes.sort("betweenness", descending=True).head(5).select( "label", "faction", "degree", "betweenness", "pagerank" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
shape: (5, 5)

``` ::: ::: The two leaders top both measures. Member 31 is the odd one out: it has only 6 ties and about a third of the leaders' PageRank, yet it ranks fifth for betweenness. Its tie to the instructor, member 0, is one of the few that cross between the factions. Sized by betweenness and colored by faction: ::: {#182f992b .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} karate.plot( size_by="betweenness", color_by="faction", label_by="label", seed=4 ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
